notes.b: The State pays income support to unemployed people through two routes, and the route decides what a claimant has to prove. All social welfare payments come from the Department of Social Protection.
points: Social insurance payments (also called benefits) depend on a record of PRSI contributions paid while in work, and they are not means-tested. They are funded from those PRSI contributions.

Social assistance payments are means-tested, which means the household's income and savings are assessed, and no contribution record is required, because they are paid on the basis of need. They are funded from general taxation.
Jobseeker's Benefit is the main social insurance payment for an unemployed person who has enough paid PRSI contributions, so the claimant's own contributions earn the right to it.
Jobseeker's Allowance is the main social assistance payment for an unemployed person who does not qualify for Jobseeker's Benefit or whose benefit has ended, so it acts as a safety net.

A Jobseeker's Allowance claimant must be unemployed, capable of work, available for full-time work and genuinely seeking employment. This shows the payment supports people who want work, not people who have chosen not to work.
Supplementary Welfare Allowance is a means-tested payment for people with no or very low income whose basic needs are not met. It also pays exceptional needs.
notes.tip: Social insurance is not means-tested and social assistance is, and examiners reward you for stating that difference. For a named payment, give its name, who it is for, how it is paid (contributions or means test) and what it provides. Quote no payment amounts.

notes.b: Families with children face extra costs, so several payments are aimed at them. Some reach every family, and others are limited to low-income households.
points: Child Benefit is paid for each qualifying child regardless of the parents' income. It is universal, not means-tested, so it reaches families on every income level.
Payments for lone parents are means-tested, because they are aimed at those in need, and recognise that one adult is carrying the full cost of the household.

The Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement) is a tax-free, means-tested weekly payment for low-paid workers who have a dependent child. It is an in-work payment, so it makes work pay and eases the poverty trap.
Means-tested payments are reduced as income rises, so the household gains less from extra earnings than the wage itself.
The Fuel Allowance is paid weekly to qualifying low-income households during the winter season to help with heating costs, which rise in cold weather.
notes.tip: Child Benefit is universal and is neither insurance nor means-tested. Fuel Allowance and the Working Family Payment are means-tested. If asked about the Working Family Payment, call it that, not Family Income Supplement.

notes.h: Schemes that reduce expenditure for low-income families
notes.b: Besides cash payments, the State lowers the cost of essentials such as health, school, housing and childcare for families on low incomes. Each scheme either pays for something or removes a cost.
points: Medical card: gives free GP visits and access to many health services, run by the HSE. Eligibility depends on income and, in some cases, health needs.

Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance: a once-yearly payment, because the cost falls at the start of the school year, that helps qualifying families meet the cost of school uniforms and shoes.
Household Benefits Package: help with electricity or gas and a free television licence for qualifying older people and people with certain disabilities or long-term illnesses.

Housing supports: local authority (social) housing is let at rents related to income. The Housing Assistance Payment (HAP) is paid through the local authority to help households pay rent in the private rented sector, and the tenant's rent contribution is based on income.

Education supports: the school meals programme and free school book schemes ease the cost of school, and the free pre-school place (ECCE), an early-learning place before primary school, reduces childcare costs.

Money Advice and Budgeting Service (MABS): a free, confidential, State-funded service, working under the Citizens Information Board, that helps people in debt, mainly low-income households, to budget and deal with creditors.
notes.tip: When asked for one scheme to reduce expenditure, name it first, say who qualifies (low income or a special need) and say what it pays for or removes, giving two details. Medical card, Fuel Allowance and the Back to School Allowance are means-tested supports, not insurance payments.

notes.b: These initiatives work through training, business supports and job creation rather than income support alone. A statutory body is one set up by law or run by the State.
points: SOLAS is the State further education and training authority. It funds, plans and coordinates further education and training through the Education and Training Boards (ETBs).
SOLAS supports apprenticeships, vocational courses and literacy, numeracy and digital training, and it provides skills training and upskilling, matching the skills of unemployed people to vacancies.
Enterprise Ireland is the State agency that helps Irish-owned companies increase sales, exports and employment through grants, market advice and training. More sales and exports create jobs.
Local Enterprise Offices (LEOs) in each county are the first stop shop for people starting or growing small businesses, giving training, mentoring, advice and grants and encouraging job creation.
Intreo is the Department of Social Protection's public employment service. It gives job-seekers advice, job-matching and referral to training, so unemployed people can be linked to vacancies.
Work-based learning and CV and job-search preparation give unemployed people the experience that employers ask for, which makes them more employable.

Community Employment (CE) offers temporary part-time work placements on local community projects for long-term unemployed and other eligible people. It is a Department of Social Protection scheme, not a SOLAS one.

Other schemes that support a return to education and training are the Vocational Training Opportunities Scheme (VTOS), the Back to Education Allowance and Youthreach, an ETB programme for early school leavers.
notes.tip: For a statutory initiative, name the body, say what it is, then give two functions and show how each creates jobs or improves employment prospects. Name SOLAS, Enterprise Ireland or a Local Enterprise Office, and do not name replaced bodies even if an old marking scheme does.

notes.h: Initiatives encouraging foreign investment (Higher Level only)
notes.b: Foreign direct investment (FDI) is investment by an overseas company that sets up or expands operations in Ireland. The State encourages it because it creates jobs, but it also brings risks.
points: IDA Ireland is the State agency responsible for attracting overseas companies and for helping foreign companies already here to expand, through grants, site selection and advice.
A low corporation tax rate is a key incentive for multinational companies to locate in Ireland: 12.5%, and 15% for the largest multinational groups.
Other attractions are a young, skilled, flexible, educated and English-speaking workforce, grant assistance, good telecommunications and access to the European Union's single market.
Foreign investment, for example a new plant, creates direct jobs in the foreign firms and indirect jobs in suppliers and services, so it reduces unemployment.
It also brings tax revenue and new skills and technology into local labour markets, so workers can move on to other employers.
Dependence on a few large multinationals is a weakness: if a parent company closes or moves a plant, a local area can lose many jobs at once.
Multinational employment tends to be concentrated in larger towns and cities, so rural areas benefit less from it. IDA Ireland aims to spread investment to regions outside the main cities.
notes.tip: For foreign investment, name IDA Ireland, give why multinationals come, and state the risk of dependence on a few large firms.

keyTerms.definition: State payments funded by PRSI contributions, available to people with a sufficient contribution record.
State payments made on the basis of need, which are means-tested and do not depend on a contribution record.
An assessment of a household's income, savings and circumstances that decides whether, and how much, a payment is made.
A means-tested payment for an unemployed person who is capable of and available for work and does not qualify for Jobseeker's Benefit.
A card giving free GP visits and other health services to people who meet income-based eligibility rules.
Investment by an overseas company in a business or facility in Ireland, such as a new factory or office.
The State agency that attracts and supports overseas companies investing in Ireland.
The State agency that supports Irish-owned companies to grow their sales, exports and employment.
A tax-free, means-tested payment for low-paid working families with a dependent child.
A means-tested payment, made through the local authority, that helps households pay rent in the private rented sector.

factCards.definition: Social insurance depends on a record of PRSI contributions; social assistance is means-tested and does not depend on contributions.

factCards.definition: Being unemployed, capable of work, available for full-time work and genuinely seeking employment.

factCards.term: Payment made to every qualifying child regardless of parental income
In-work support for low-paid families with a dependent child

It helps qualifying households meet heating costs during the winter season.

factCards.term: Three benefits of the free pre-school place (ECCE)
factCards.definition: It reduces childcare costs for families; it prepares children for primary school; it builds social and learning skills.

factCards.definition: IDA Ireland, which offers grants, site selection and advice to multinational firms.

factCards.definition: It creates direct jobs in the area; it brings tax revenue and new skills into the local economy.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between social insurance and social assistance payments, giving one example of each.
questions.model: Social insurance payments depend on a record of PRSI contributions paid while in work and are not means-tested. Example: Jobseeker's Benefit for a worker who has lost a job and has enough paid contributions. Social assistance payments are based on need, assessed through a means test of the household's income and savings, and do not depend on contributions. Example: Jobseeker's Allowance for an unemployed person who does not qualify for Jobseeker's Benefit.

questions.prompt: Discuss the statutory responses to poverty in Ireland. Refer to social welfare payments, at least one scheme that reduces costs for low-income families, and the role of foreign investment in creating employment.
questions.model: Social welfare: social insurance payments depend on PRSI contributions, while social assistance payments such as Jobseeker's Allowance and Supplementary Welfare Allowance are means-tested and paid on the basis of need; Child Benefit is universal for each qualifying child; the Working Family Payment supports low-paid working families with a dependent child. Schemes reducing costs: the medical card gives free GP visits to those who meet income and health criteria; the Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance helps with uniforms and shoes; the Fuel Allowance helps with heating costs; the Housing Assistance Payment helps with rent in the private rented sector; the free pre-school place (ECCE) reduces childcare costs. Each scheme addresses a specific cost pressure that would otherwise push a family into poverty. Foreign investment: foreign direct investment is investment by overseas companies in Irish operations; IDA Ireland attracts it with grants, site selection and advice; a low corporation tax rate and a skilled, English-speaking workforce are key attractions; it creates direct jobs, tax revenue and new skills, reducing unemployment. Limitations: dependence on a few large multinationals exposes local areas to sudden job losses when plants close; multinational jobs are concentrated in larger towns and cities, so rural areas gain less. Assessment: income supports relieve immediate hardship, while investment and employment supports address the root cause of unemployment, so the two work best together.
